title: US Employers Rewrite the H-1B Playbook as Immigration Costs Soar
excerpt: Companies are accelerating green card timelines, building student visa pipelines, and moving talent offshore as rising costs and policy shifts make the H-1B program harder to navigate.
body:
• Nearly 60% of US employers submitted more H-1B registrations than the previous year despite tighter selection rules, according to Envoy Global's 2026 survey of 519 HR professionals.
  • Three out of four employers now initiate green card sponsorship within the first three months of employment, a sharp acceleration from historical timelines.
  • 65% of companies reported losing foreign national employees who left the US due to visa issues, up from 53% in 2025.
  • 68% of employers expect to turn to nearshoring or offshoring in 2026 to manage immigration barriers and labor shortages.

US employers are fundamentally restructuring how they recruit and retain foreign professionals as the Trump administration's immigration overhaul makes the H-1B program significantly more expensive and unpredictable, according to a major new industry survey.

The Envoy Global U.S. Corporate Immigration Trends 2026 Report, based on a survey of 519 HR and global mobility professionals, shows that companies are no longer treating H-1B sponsorship as a standalone process. Instead, employers are building multi-year immigration strategies that begin with student visas, extend through H-1B sponsorship, and culminate in earlier green card applications.

"A little over six months into 2026, the immigration landscape already looks markedly different from what employers anticipated a year ago."

— Jason Brennan, CEO, Envoy Global

More Registrations, Fewer Slots

Despite a suite of policy changes — including the $100,000 H-1B consular processing fee, a wage-weighted cap selection system, and proposed prevailing wage hikes — demand for H-1B talent remains strong. Nearly six in ten employers submitted more registrations than the previous year, even as US Citizenship and Immigration Services accepted fewer overall.

But the headline numbers mask a structural shift. Sherry Neal, partner at Envoy Global, cautioned that higher registration volumes do not necessarily reflect new hiring. "In many cases, employers are re-registering candidates who were not selected in previous H-1B lotteries," she said. Companies employing workers on OPT and STEM OPT extensions routinely submit registrations for those employees every year alongside new candidates, creating a compounding backlog effect.

The Student Visa Pipeline

Recognizing the uncertainty surrounding the H-1B lottery, employers are aggressively strengthening their student visa pipeline. The survey found that 93% of employers support foreign national employees through F-1 work authorization programs, including OPT, STEM OPT, and Curricular Practical Training. Of those, 39% support both OPT and STEM OPT filings, while 35% support OPT-only filings.

"The widespread majority of employers supporting F-1 OPT and STEM OPT filings reflects the critical role student visa pathways play in addressing talent gaps in the US workforce, particularly in technical and specialized roles," said Anne Walsh, partner at Envoy Global. She noted that STEM OPT gives employers additional time to plan H-1B sponsorship and that companies increasingly view F-1 pathways as part of a multi-year immigration strategy.

Green Cards in Three Months

The report documents a significant shift in permanent residence planning. Three out of four employers now initiate green card sponsorship within the first three months of employment — a dramatic acceleration from timelines of a decade ago when companies often waited years before beginning the process.

"Two main factors likely drive employers' decision to speed up green card sponsorship — long processing times and uncertainty about non-immigrant visas," said Rita Ambrosetti, partner at Envoy Global. Rising H-1B costs, including the $100,000 fee and increased scrutiny of petitions, are creating greater urgency to secure permanent residency earlier.

Premium processing has become a near-universal safeguard: 83% of employers use it, covering nearly three out of four H-1B petition categories on average. It is most commonly applied to extensions and renewals (78%), initial cap petitions (77%), and transfers (70%).

The Talent Drain

The policy shifts are already driving measurable talent losses. Some 65% of employers reported that foreign national employees left the US due to visa-related issues in the past year, up from 53% in 2025. Meanwhile, 61% said they relocated employees outside the US due to visa barriers, a sharp increase from 49% a year earlier.

Looking ahead, 68% of employers expect to turn to nearshoring or offshoring in 2026 to manage immigration barriers and labor shortages — a trend that runs counter to the administration's stated goal of keeping skilled jobs in the United States.

What It Means for Indian Workers

The changes carry outsized implications for Indian nationals, who represent the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries and face the longest green card backlogs. The wage-weighted lottery, which went into effect on February 27, gives higher odds to workers placed in the top wage levels — potentially disadvantaging younger Indian professionals entering the US workforce at entry or mid-level salaries.

For Indian IT services firms, the $100,000 fee on new petitions filed from abroad has made the traditional model of rotating workers from India significantly more expensive, accelerating conversations about offshoring and remote delivery.

Despite the upheaval, the H-1B remains indispensable. "The H-1B remains the most common visa category because it is the only broadly applicable pathway that spans all industries, company structure and size, and worker nationalities," Neal said.
nri_angle: Indian nationals, the largest H-1B beneficiary group, face heightened risks from wage-weighted lottery changes and the dollar100K fee that makes rotating workers from India far more expensive.
